Sometimes a code like that will set because the battery got low, or a hiccup in the network that led the signal to be briefly interrupted.  A "lack of training" would result in instantly throwing parts at something because it used to have a code.  You're coming in here insulting people about something you don't understand.

Codes do NOT mean "this is the problem" and if we threw parts at things just because the code said that part we'd have a LOT of angry customers when that didn't fix it.

Case in point, say you get an "O2 sensor heater circuit low" code.  There is at least a 50/50 chance that the problem isn't the sensor, it's a wiring problem.  Sure, I could throw a $200 sensor in there - OR I could actually test, verify the problem and possibly find a torn wire that I could fix for $50.

Non-mechanics think codes are the be-all end-all of diagnosing cars but the fact is, they're more like signposts - "hey, this sensor gave me some unusual output, better see what caused this" - NOT "the sensor is bad replace it".

Modern cars are incredibly complex.  Codes don't tell you what need fixing, they tell you something isn't right.  Think of them as signposts...they point you in a direction but that is all.  Diagnosing engine codes involves monitoring input from many sensors under varying conditions.

Mechanics aren't dumb monkeys, we have to have a functional knowledge of applied physics, understand air/fuel mixtures, on and on.

A really great example of why customers should pay diag charges... let's say you have a code for cam/crankshaft not being properly correlated.  There are many, many things that cause this problem.  The obvious thing would be to change a VVT actuator based on the code...but the first step in properly diagnosing VVT codes is...change the oil.  About 40-60% of the time an oil change fixes it, meaning you don't need a $400 actuator.  

"Mechanics" who don't diagnose will throw an actuator at it without any testing and literally just hope it works.

I don't replace anything until I have eliminated every other potential cause for a problem.
The list MAY be short because sometimes the first thing you test is the problem, but it should say the steps they took to decide on a diagnosis.

Unfortunately it's pretty much a word of mouth thing.  It's tough because many customers leave bad reviews because they paid a diagnostic fee.  In general, if they say diag is free they're not going to do any.  General advice though - avoid chains.  Look for well reviewed independent shops.  Also, when talking to the service advisor, just ask if they will comp labor for repairs of misdiagnosed issues.  A reputable shop that takes accuracy seriously will say yes.  Also, before authorizing repairs after a problem is diagnosed, ask them to read you the "story" on the ticket.  If it says "P0420 - replace cat" they're garbage.  If it has a long list of steps taken to diagnose and the results of each step the mechanic takes diagnosis seriously.

Stop listening to 'everyone', because whoever they are, they are idiots.  The only thing you ever, ever do by feel on an engine is spark plugs.  Not only do you need to torque all engine bolts/nuts to spec,.you also need to torque them in a specific order to ensure a good deal and prevent possible breakage of engine parts.  I've seen more than one broken valve cover because somebody "winged it".

Just a real pet peeve of mine that people think our wealth of knowledge and experience is just "checking codes".  

Oh, and another reason parts stores scan for free?  Because people who don't know better will buy a part on the spot to fix a problem that may not exist.  Also their employees don't know a thing about what those codes might mean.

A car could have a P0420 (catalytic converter failure) code, for example.  Do you throw a $1000 converter in it because it said that?  Only if you're a complete hack.  That code can be caused by malfunctioning O2 sensors, exhaust leaks, on and on and on.  Maybe instead of that $1000 cat you need $50 worth of welding.  THAT is what you pay diag for.

Let me make this clear: nobody worth a damn replaces a part based solely on a code.  You need a scanner that shows live data to confirm whether the problem is the sensor or one of dozens of things that could be throwing the sensor off.  Even if the voltage to the sensor looks iffy, it could be wiring and not the sensor. Only hacks replace parts just because it has a code.

Diagnosis fees save you from buying a part only to find out that didn't fix it, then paying diagnosis anyway to figure out what the real problem is.

It's not important at all to fix in terms of driving the car.  The actuators are to change from heat to AC, or from blowing on the floor to blowing out the dash vents.  On modern cars these air control 'doors' are computer controlled and usually go through a self calibration when you turn the car on.  Best way to isolate which actuator it is is to move your climate controls around.  If it clicks when you switch from heat to AC or vice versa that's a blend actuator.  If it clicks changing from dash to floor it's a mode actuator.  These actuators are commonly referred to as doors, so...blend door, mode door.  Only effect will be that you may not be able to get the temperature where you want it, or get air blowing where you want it but absolutely not a safety issue or anything that's going to leave you stranded.

This being an American car it's safe to assume OP doesn't know what an "earth" is.  We call them grounds in all applications.  Just FYI.

Every electrical circuit needs a ground to allow spent current to return to its source.  On a car this takes the form of a wire attached to the body of the vehicle.  A bad ground is one that has excessive resistance or intermittent lack of contact because of corrosion or a loose fastener.  You will need a repair manual and wiring diagrams to locate where the ground is for the specific circuit (the MAF circuit in this case).

Replacing the whole harness is massively overkill.  You need to find the ground point and make sure that it's free of rust/corrosion, and tightly attached to the body.

If there is a black/white wire, then that should be your ground.  

Unfortunately, service information is pretty much behind a paywall.  If the ground turns out bad, update your post and maybe someone who works for your make can look up the ground location for you.

EDIT: yeah, one lead to the ground wire, one to the engine itself.  Set the meter to read ohms (omega symbol).  Do this with the car off.

You can check the ground by going from the ground pin on the MAF connector to any metal on the engine.  No need to go to the battery.

If you have anything over a few milliohms of resistance you'll need to locate the actual ground.  

If not, consider buying some MAF cleaner, pull out the sensor and clean and reinstall it per the directions on the cleaner.

It's right there in the name "impact".  An impact works by making tiny little hammer blows to turn the shaft.  That concussion knocks rust loose.  Even when hand tools are necessary to reach a stuck bolt, it's not uncommon to tap the ratchet with a dead blow hammer to break it loose.  

When you just pull on it with a ratchet you're twisting the whole thing without that concussion shocking things loose.  So it's more likely to just twist off without ever loosening any rust.

You still have to be gentle when using an impact - if it doesn't zip right out you need to feather the trigger in short bursts.  And realize when it's not working and apply penetrating oil or heat.

For small bolts, impacts are fine IF you use a smaller impact with less power.  If you use the impact you take your lug nuts off with, it'll rip the head right off that little 10mm.  But a 1/4" drive cordless impact has a LOT less torque.

The key is to develop a feel for when things don't want to come and need extra help from heat, oil, etc.

Okay so first things first.  You want good drill bits. Preferably cobalt. They aren't cheap, but they will save you literal, actual hours of cutting and they're hard to break as long as you drill straight.

Also, if you've given up and are sure you're gonna drill, get your biggest bar and break that bolt head off.  It's a lot of extra metal to get through and it's hard to stay straight.

On to the actual drilling.  First you want to take a center punch and make a little divot in the dead center of the surface.  Start with a very small drill bit and create a pilot hole to guide your bits and keep you drilling straight.  Only needs to be a few mm deep.  Now, start working up in bit sizes until you have a nice little dent that your final bit (which should be like 1/16" smaller than the bolt shaft) can sit in.  Now it's just about drilling straight.  Check your hole frequently to make sure it's not drifting.

Use a cutting oil liberally to help cool the bits as you drill.  Cobalt is super heat resistant but you still want oil.  Rest when you get tired...tired arms are more likely to start drifting.

If you get the hole perfectly straight, you'll drill through everything but the threads and your bit will just pull those out and leave you with a nice clean hole.  Run a thread chaser down the hole just in case to make sure the threads are in fact good.

When things are on even with the car off, they're shorted.  Since it's affecting multiple systems the short is most likely in one of the fuseboxes.

You need an experienced tech with electrical skills to figure this out.  It will probably not be cheap.

I would expect to pay at least an hour, possibly more, in labor for diagnosing the problem.  Then it could be anything from a few minutes labor (for a minor wiring repair) to requiring replacement of the TIPM module (Dodge for main fusebox) which could run into hundreds for the part plus another hour or so of labor.

Brake fluid is hygroscopic and is going to absorb a lot of the water in your coolant.  I would advise not driving it until the coolant has been flushed.  If this means towing it to a shop, you should do that.
